name: Breadcutter Choke from Side Control
description: Master the Breadcutter Choke from Side Control. Learn gi collar grip mechanics, finishing details, and defensive counters for this high-percentage blood choke.
summary: The Breadcutter Choke from Side Control is a gi blood choke where the top player feeds a collar deep behind the opponent's neck and drives the forearm across the throat, scissoring both carotid arteries to force a rapid tap.
overview:
The Breadcutter Choke from Side Control is a devastating gi-based blood choke that leverages the perpendicular alignment of standard side control to establish deep collar grips behind the opponent's neck. This submission exploits a mechanical advantage unique to side control: the attacker's body weight can be driven directly through the choking forearm while the collar grip creates a fixed fulcrum against the far-side carotid artery. The result is a scissors-like compression of both carotid arteries that produces rapid unconsciousness if not defended.

The setup rewards patience and positional dominance. From established side control, the attacker feeds the near-side lapel deep behind the opponent's neck with the cross-side hand, threading the fabric under the neck and securing a four-finger grip on the far collar as deep as possible. The finishing hand then reaches across the opponent's throat to grip the near-side lapel, creating the characteristic cross-collar configuration. The choke is completed by sprawling the hips away while driving the forearm across the neck and pulling the behind-the-neck grip upward.

This choke is particularly effective because opponents under side control typically prioritize defending arm attacks and preventing mount transitions, leaving the collar relatively accessible. The breadcutter can be set up incrementally during normal pressure maintenance, with the critical behind-the-neck grip established over several seconds before the opponent recognizes the threat. When combined with strong crossface pressure and hip control, the choke becomes extremely difficult to defend once both grips are secured.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate with proper release; prolonged compression can cause serious injury

injury_risks.injury: Tracheal damage from misaligned forearm pressure or sudden force
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-6 weeks for minor damage; surgery required for severe cases

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain or cervical spine stress from resistance under pressure
Jaw or facial pressure causing TMJ irritation

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training, never spike or jerk
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any distress vocalization)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body
Any rapid tapping motion with hand or foot
release_protocol: Immediately release collar grip upon tap signal
Remove body weight and pressure from opponent's neck
Allow opponent to turn to safe position (typically supine or seated)
Check that opponent is breathing normally and conscious
Give partner time to recover before continuing training
training_restrictions: Never apply competition speed or force in training
Never spike or jerk the choke - always apply gradually
Always ensure partner has clear access to tap
Stop immediately at any sign of distress, even without tap
Never practice on partners with neck or throat injuries
Beginners must drill under supervision for first 20+ repetitions

variations_and_setups.description: From side control with crossface, the top hand feeds the opponent's far lapel behind their neck while maintaining chest pressure. The bottom hand receives the lapel for a deep four-finger grip before the cross-collar finishing grip is established.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Default entry when you have stable side control with crossface and the opponent is relatively flat on their back

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Paper Cutter Variation with Near Lapel
variations_and_setups.description: Instead of feeding the far lapel, grip the near-side lapel first and thread it across the opponent's throat before establishing the behind-the-neck grip. This variation disguises the choke setup as normal collar control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent is protecting their far collar or when you want to disguise the choke within normal grip fighting

variations_and_setups.description: Begin with a standard crossface underhook and incrementally walk your hand from the underhook position up to the collar behind the neck. This gradual transition makes the choke setup less detectable.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against experienced opponents who recognize and defend direct collar grabs immediately

attacker.name: from Side Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Breadcutter Choke from Side Control. Step-by-step collar grip setup, finishing mechanics, and counter strategies for this gi choke.
attacker.overview: The Breadcutter Choke from Side Control rewards methodical grip establishment and heavy pressure. As the attacker, your primary objective is to thread the far-side lapel behind the opponent's neck without telegraphing the choke setup. This requires maintaining dominant side control throughout the grip-fighting sequence, using crossface pressure to keep the opponent flat while your hands work incrementally toward the collar. The finish combines a sprawl with a forearm drive across the neck, amplified by body weight dropping through the choking arm. Patience is essential because rushing the grip setup alerts the defender and allows them to strip your grips before the choke is locked.
key_principles: Maintain heavy crossface pressure throughout the entire setup to prevent the opponent from turning into you or creating defensive frames
Feed the lapel incrementally behind the neck rather than making one obvious reaching motion that telegraphs the attack
Establish the behind-the-neck grip as deep as possible before attempting the cross grip, as depth determines finishing power
Use body weight through the forearm rather than arm strength alone to generate choking pressure during the finish
Keep hips sprawled and heavy during the finishing sequence to prevent the opponent from bridging or creating space
Treat the collar setup as part of normal side control maintenance to disguise the attack until both grips are secured
setup_requirements: Established side control with chest-to-chest pressure and crossface driving the opponent's face away
Opponent relatively flat on their back with limited ability to turn or create angles
Near-side knee tight against the opponent's hip to block guard recovery during the grip-fighting phase
Access to at least one side of the opponent's gi collar without immediate grip stripping
Sufficient control to free one hand for the lapel feed while maintaining positional dominance with the other

execution_steps.description: Secure heavy side control with strong crossface pressure driving the opponent's face away from you. Your near-side knee presses tight against their hip, and your chest is perpendicular to theirs with maximum contact. Settle your weight before initiating any grip changes.

With your top hand (closest to opponent's head), reach across and grip the opponent's far-side lapel at collar level. Pull the lapel loose from their belt and begin threading the fabric behind their neck toward your bottom hand. Use small incremental pulls rather than one large motion.

Your bottom hand (closest to opponent's hips) reaches under to receive the threaded lapel. Secure a deep four-finger grip on the far collar behind the neck, pulling as much slack out of the fabric as possible. The deeper this grip, the more powerful the eventual choke.

With the behind-the-neck grip locked, your top hand now reaches across the opponent's throat to grip the near-side lapel at approximately collarbone level. Use a four-finger-in grip with your forearm blade positioned directly across the throat or jawline. This creates the cross-collar scissors configuration.

Shift your weight slightly toward the opponent's head and begin sprawling your hips back and away. Your choking forearm should be positioned so the blade of the forearm contacts the opponent's throat. Keep your head low and chest heavy to prevent the opponent from sitting up or bridging.

Sprawl your hips fully away from the opponent while simultaneously pulling upward with the behind-the-neck grip and driving downward and across with the cross-collar forearm. Drop your chest weight through the choking arm to maximize bilateral carotid compression. The opposing forces create a scissors action.

Hold the finishing position with steady increasing pressure, keeping your hips sprawled and weight committed through the forearm. Monitor continuously for tap signals including verbal taps, physical taps, and body going limp. Release immediately upon any tap signal. The choke should produce a tap within three to five seconds of full application.

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips the behind-the-neck collar grip before it is fully established
common_counters.your_response: Revert to crossface pressure and re-establish side control. Attempt the lapel feed again using smaller incremental movements or switch to a different collar entry angle. Consider using the crossface-to-collar transition variation.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and shrimps to create space during the grip-fighting phase
common_counters.your_response: Follow their hip movement with your hips, maintaining chest pressure. If they create significant space, abandon the choke and consolidate side control. Their bridging often opens opportunities for mount transition or knee on belly.

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you and recovers guard during the finishing sprawl
common_counters.your_response: If they turn before the choke is locked, maintain the collar grip and look for a loop choke or cross collar choke from inside their guard. If the grips are lost, work to pass guard and re-establish side control.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin and blocks forearm from crossing the throat
common_counters.your_response: Drive the forearm across the jawline instead. The jaw acts as a lever to expose the neck. Alternatively, use the crossface hand to push their chin up before sliding the forearm into position across the throat.

common_errors.error: Attempting the choke before establishing dominant side control with settled weight
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes during the grip-fighting phase because positional control is insufficient to prevent movement, wasting the choke setup entirely
common_errors.correction: Spend five to ten seconds settling heavy side control with crossface and hip pressure before initiating any collar grip work

common_errors.error: Feeding the lapel too shallow behind the neck, leaving slack in the fabric
common_errors.consequence: The choke lacks finishing power because the collar does not compress the far-side carotid artery effectively, allowing the opponent to survive and defend
common_errors.correction: Pull maximum slack out of the collar before securing the behind-the-neck grip. The deeper the grip, the less distance needed to close the choke

common_errors.error: Lifting hips during the finish instead of sprawling away
common_errors.consequence: Creates space under your body that the opponent exploits to bridge, insert a knee, or turn to recover guard
common_errors.correction: Sprawl hips back and away while keeping chest weight committed through the choking forearm. Hips should move away from the opponent, not upward

common_errors.error: Telegraphing the setup by reaching obviously and quickly for the far collar
common_errors.consequence: Experienced opponents immediately strip the grip or begin escape sequences before the choke is established
common_errors.correction: Integrate the collar feed into normal side control grip adjustments. Use small incremental movements and transition gradually from crossface to collar control

common_errors.error: Relying on arm strength to squeeze the choke rather than body weight and sprawl mechanics
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly and the choke pressure is insufficient against larger or stronger opponents, burning grip endurance for no finish
common_errors.correction: Drive body weight through the forearm by sprawling and dropping chest. The arms maintain grip while the body generates the choking force

common_errors.error: Releasing crossface pressure prematurely while transitioning to collar grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent turns toward you or creates frames that block collar access and may lead to guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Maintain head control with your shoulder and chest pressure even as your hands transition to collar grips. Never leave the head uncontrolled

training_progressions.description: Practice the lapel feed and behind-the-neck grip with a cooperative partner. Focus on pulling maximum slack, establishing deep four-finger grips, and transitioning smoothly between crossface control and collar access. Repeat 30 times per side with no resistance.

With grips pre-established, drill the finishing sequence focusing on sprawl direction, forearm blade placement across the neck, and body weight commitment through the choking arm. Partner provides light resistance and taps early to build timing awareness.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Full Sequence with Moderate Resistance
training_progressions.description: Execute the complete sequence from side control establishment through the finish with a partner providing moderate resistance. Partner defends collar grips at fifty percent and practices tapping appropriately. Focus on reading defensive reactions and adjusting grip angles.

training_progressions.focus: Integration into rolling and positional sparring
training_progressions.description: Apply the breadcutter in positional sparring starting from side control. Partner defends with full resistance. Develop ability to chain the choke with other attacks when the collar grip is stripped, and recognize optimal timing windows during transitions.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Breadcutter Choke primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The Breadcutter Choke primarily compresses both carotid arteries using a scissors-like action between the behind-the-neck collar grip and the cross-collar forearm. The collar pulls against one carotid while the forearm drives across the other, creating bilateral vascular compression that restricts blood flow to the brain.

flashcards.question: Why is the depth of the behind-the-neck collar grip critical to finishing the choke?
flashcards.answer: A deeper grip behind the neck means less distance is required to close the choking mechanism and more of the collar fabric contacts the far-side carotid artery. A shallow grip leaves slack that the opponent can exploit to create defensive space, and the collar may slide off the artery during the finishing sprawl, reducing compression effectiveness significantly.

flashcards.question: What control must be maintained before initiating the collar feed to prevent escape?
flashcards.answer: You must have established heavy side control with crossface pressure driving the opponent's face away, chest-to-chest perpendicular contact, and your near knee blocking their far hip. Without settled positional control, the opponent will escape during the grip transition phase when one of your hands is occupied with the lapel feed rather than controlling their body.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin tightly to block the forearm from crossing the throat - how do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Drive the forearm blade across the jawline rather than directly across the throat. The jaw acts as a lever that forces the chin up and exposes the neck. Alternatively, use the crossface hand to push their chin upward before sliding the choking forearm into position. The chin tuck defense becomes ineffective once the forearm gains purchase on the jaw.

flashcards.question: What happens if the opponent bridges explosively during your finishing sprawl?
flashcards.answer: If the grips are fully secured, maintain the sprawl and ride the bridge by keeping chest weight committed through the forearm. The bridge actually helps close the choke if your position is correct. If the grips are not fully set, the bridge may create enough space for them to turn in and recover guard, so you must abandon the choke and secure side control.

flashcards.question: Why should you never spike or jerk the Breadcutter Choke during training?
flashcards.answer: Sudden explosive force on the neck can cause tracheal damage, cervical spine injury, and carotid artery trauma that may require surgery and weeks to months of recovery. Blood chokes compress the carotid arteries and can cause unconsciousness within seconds, so a gradual controlled application gives the training partner adequate time to recognize the choke and tap before losing consciousness.

flashcards.question: What is the proper release protocol when your partner taps to the Breadcutter Choke?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release the collar grip upon any tap signal, including verbal, physical hand or foot tap, or body going limp. Remove body weight and pressure from the opponent's neck, allow them to turn to a safe position, verify they are breathing normally and conscious, and give them recovery time before continuing. Never hold the choke even momentarily after a tap.

flashcards.question: How does the Breadcutter Choke chain with other attacks when the opponent defends the collar grip?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent focuses on stripping collar grips, their arms move away from their body and their attention shifts to hand fighting. This opens opportunities for americana and kimura attacks on the exposed arms, arm triangle setups when they bring an arm across their neck defensively, and transitions to mount or knee on belly while they are occupied with grip defense rather than positional escape.

defender.name: from Side Control Defender
defender.description: Defend the Breadcutter Choke from Side Control. Recognition cues, grip prevention, escape techniques, and guard recovery strategies for bottom players.
defender.overview: Defending the Breadcutter Choke from Side Control requires early recognition of collar grip attempts before the attacker establishes the behind-the-neck grip. Once both collar grips are secured and the attacker begins the finishing sprawl, escape becomes extremely difficult due to the combined weight and collar pressure. The defensive priority hierarchy is clear: first prevent the initial deep collar feed by keeping elbows tight and controlling the attacker's wrists, second strip any partial collar grips before the cross grip is established, and third work guard recovery before the finishing sprawl pins you flat. When caught in the choke, immediate collar grip stripping combined with aggressive hip movement toward the attacker offers the best survival chance.
key_principles: Monitor the attacker's hands constantly for any movement toward your collar, as the choke cannot be finished without the behind-the-neck collar grip
Keep elbows tight to your body to block the attacker's hand path to your collar and deny the lapel feed behind your neck
Strip collar grips immediately when detected rather than waiting to see if the attacker commits to the choke
Turn toward the attacker rather than away when defending the choke, as turning away exposes more of the collar and neck
Create frames against the attacker's choking arm the moment the cross-collar grip is established to prevent the forearm from settling across your throat
Prioritize guard recovery over simple survival, using defensive movements to simultaneously create space for knee insertion
recognition_cues: Attacker's top hand releases the crossface or underhook and reaches toward your far-side collar or lapel
Feeling fabric being pulled and threaded behind your neck as the attacker feeds the lapel under your head
Attacker's bottom hand moves from hip control to reach under your neck for the collar grip
Attacker shifts weight toward your head and begins sprawling hips backward away from your body
Cross-collar forearm pressure settling across your throat or jawline with the attacker's wrist rotating inward

defensive_options.action: Strip the behind-the-neck collar grip with both hands before the cross grip is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the lapel being threaded behind your neck or detect the attacker's hand reaching for your far collar
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker loses the primary grip and must restart the choke setup from scratch, returning to standard side control
defensive_options.risk: Both hands committed to grip stripping temporarily removes your frames, opening a brief window for mount advancement

defensive_options.action: Hip escape toward the attacker and insert knee for half guard recovery while they focus on collar grips
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker removes a controlling hand from your hip to establish collar grips, creating momentary hip freedom
defensive_options.if_successful: You recover guard and neutralize the choke threat entirely by breaking the perpendicular alignment needed for the finish
defensive_options.risk: If the collar grip is already deep, turning in may tighten the choke rather than alleviate it

defensive_options.action: Frame against the choking forearm with both hands and bridge toward the attacker to create space
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the cross-collar grip is established and the attacker begins the finishing sprawl with forearm across your throat
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough space to push the forearm off your throat and strip the cross grip, forcing the attacker back to positional control
defensive_options.risk: Bridging toward the attacker may help them advance to mount if the choke fails and they capitalize on the space you create

escape_paths: Strip the behind-the-neck collar grip with two hands on the wrist, then immediately re-establish defensive frames against the attacker's shoulders to prevent re-establishment
Hip escape toward the attacker while pushing the choking forearm off your neck, inserting your near knee between bodies to recover half guard or closed guard
Bridge explosively toward the attacker to disrupt their sprawl position, then use the space created to turn into them and pummel for an underhook or guard recovery

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip collar grips and immediately hip escape toward the attacker, inserting your knee and recovering closed guard before they can re-establish side control grips

Successfully strip all collar grips and re-establish defensive frames, forcing the attacker to abandon the choke and return to standard side control maintenance where you continue working systematic escapes

common_errors.error: Ignoring the initial lapel feed behind the neck and focusing only on positional escape
common_errors.consequence: The attacker establishes the deep behind-the-neck grip unopposed, making the choke setup nearly complete before you begin defending it
common_errors.correction: Monitor both of the attacker's hands at all times. The moment a hand moves toward your collar, immediately use both hands to strip the grip before it locks in

common_errors.error: Turning away from the attacker when feeling collar pressure behind the neck
common_errors.consequence: Turning away exposes more of your collar and neck, tightens the existing grip, and may give up back control if the attacker follows your rotation
common_errors.correction: Turn toward the attacker rather than away. Turning in compresses the collar space and makes it harder for the attacker to thread the lapel deeper behind your neck

common_errors.error: Pushing the attacker's head or chest with extended arms during the choke defense
common_errors.consequence: Extended arms expose your limbs to kimura and americana submissions while doing little to address the collar grip that is the actual choking mechanism
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight and frame specifically against the choking forearm and the attacker's collar-gripping wrist rather than pushing against their upper body

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to address the choke, hoping it will not be tight enough to finish
common_errors.consequence: Once both grips are secured and the sprawl begins, defensive options diminish rapidly and unconsciousness can occur within seconds
common_errors.correction: Defend the choke aggressively at the earliest possible stage. Every second of delay reduces your defensive options and increases the attacker's finishing power

flashcards.question: What is the earliest and most effective point to defend the Breadcutter Choke?
flashcards.answer: The most effective defensive window is when the attacker first attempts to feed the lapel behind your neck. At this stage, a simple two-handed grip strip on their wrist completely resets the attack. Waiting until both collar grips are established makes defense significantly harder because you must overcome both the grip strength and the attacker's body weight simultaneously.

flashcards.question: Why should you turn toward the attacker rather than away when defending this choke?
flashcards.answer: Turning toward the attacker compresses the space behind your neck, making it harder for them to feed the lapel deeper. Turning away stretches the collar across your neck, actually tightening the existing grip and exposing more of your far collar. Additionally, turning away can expose your back, creating a worse position than the original side control bottom.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Breadcutter Choke to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel bilateral pressure on both sides of your neck and cannot effectively strip either collar grip. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in as few as four to six seconds once fully locked. Do not wait to see if you can tough it out. Use verbal tap, hand tap on opponent or mat, or foot tap on mat. Tap early and tap often in training.

flashcards.question: How does the attacker releasing hip control for collar grips create a defensive opportunity?
flashcards.answer: When the attacker moves their hip-controlling hand to establish collar grips behind your neck, your hips are momentarily free from direct control. This creates a window to hip escape, insert your near knee between bodies, and recover half guard or closed guard. Recognizing this timing window is critical because the attacker cannot simultaneously control your hips and establish collar grips.

flashcards.question: What defensive structure should you maintain against your neck while under Breadcutter Choke threat?
flashcards.answer: Keep your near-side hand at collar level with fingers inside your own collar to block the attacker's hand from gripping the fabric behind your neck. Your far-side hand should be ready to strip any grip that gets past your initial defense. Elbows stay tight to your ribs to deny the hand path to the collar and maintain framing capability against the forearm if the cross grip is established.

training_progressions.description: Partner establishes side control and slowly initiates the breadcutter setup. Practice recognizing each stage: lapel feed, behind-the-neck grip, cross grip, and sprawl. Call out each stage verbally as you detect it. No resistance, pure pattern recognition at slow speed.

Partner attempts the lapel feed at moderate speed. Practice two-handed wrist control to strip the behind-the-neck grip before it locks in. Focus on timing the strip with the moment the attacker's hand moves toward the collar. Reset after each successful or failed strip attempt.

training_progressions.focus: Combining grip defense with guard recovery
training_progressions.description: Partner applies the full breadcutter setup with moderate resistance. Practice stripping grips and immediately transitioning to hip escape and guard recovery. Develop the habit of using defensive moments as escape opportunities rather than simply resetting to survival position under side control.

Start under side control with partner attacking the breadcutter at full speed and intent. Practice the complete defensive sequence from recognition through grip stripping to guard recovery against full resistance. Develop comfort with the choke pressure and confidence in your defensive timing.
